title: Optimal Finite-Time Control of Nonreciprocal Brownian Dimers: Thermodynamic Anomaly and Multiple Transitions
abstract: We solve exactly a finite-time thermodynamic optimal control problem for two nonreciprocally interacting Brownian particles translated by two harmonic traps. The controller manipulates both the center and separation of the pair. Nonreciprocal interactions generate an internal active force that couples these two channels. The optimal protocol is oscillatory, deliberately opens the dimer even when the target separation is unchanged, and can extract work during transport. A central finding is a finite critical time beyond which the external-work infimum is $-\infty$: at any prescribed duration beyond this threshold, both extractable work and output power are unbounded. Physical regularizations such as finite trap range and force saturation restore a finite optimum and convert the anomaly into optimal-protocol transitions: in the zero-target case, a hard finite range produces a first-order-like jump from the zero protocol to a maximum-range protocol, whereas smooth force saturation gives a continuous, second-order-like onset. Under finite-range constraints, the optimal protocol can further undergo multiple finite-time transitions, producing multiple work-duration kinks with no qualitative analog in prior studies.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the minimum external work required to control two interacting Brownian particles with nonreciprocal coupling. It discovers a critical time $T_c$ beyond which the extractable work becomes infinitely negative, representing a thermodynamic anomaly. By imposing realistic physical constraints like finite force range, the authors show how this anomaly resolves into distinct, measurable phase-like transitions.
main_problem: The paper solves a finite-time thermodynamic optimal control problem for two nonreciprocally interacting Brownian particles confined by harmonic traps.
main_result: Nonreciprocity leads to a 'thermodynamic anomaly' where the extractable work is unbounded below for times exceeding a critical time $T_c$. Physical regularizations restore finite optima and reveal multiple transition types.
method: The authors use optimal control theory, minimizing the mean external work functional by solving associated Euler-Lagrange equations for the system dynamics.
model_or_system: The model consists of two overdamped Brownian particles coupled by nonreciprocal interactions within harmonic traps. The control manipulates the trap centers and separation distance over time $T$.
key_observables: Mean external work ($W$), output power, optimal protocol trajectories (oscillatory), and transition points.
important_parameters: Nonreciprocity parameter ($\alpha$), critical time ($T_c$), trap range limits ($R_{	ext{max}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on solving the mean dynamics equations derived from the overdamped Langevin equation, and later introduces physical regularizations like finite force saturation or trap range.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the optimal mean paths for both reciprocal and nonreciprocal cases, and show the minimum work landscape ($W^*$) versus duration $T$ highlighting the anomaly near $T_c$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the dynamics and the work functional. It then analyzes the non-reciprocal case to find the thermodynamic anomaly at $T > T_c$. Finally, it introduces physical regularizations (finite range/saturation) to restore a finite optimum, revealing distinct transition behaviors.
why_interesting: The study of optimal control in non-equilibrium systems, especially identifying fundamental anomalies like unbounded work extraction, is highly relevant for understanding energy harvesting and dissipation in open quantum or classical many-body systems.
